questions.question: What is PreparedStatement in JDBC and why is it preferred?
questions.title: PreparedStatement in JDBC — Overview and Benefits
questions.direct_answer: A **PreparedStatement** is a precompiled, parameterized SQL statement that uses `?` placeholders bound with setter methods. It's preferred over `Statement` for two reasons: it **prevents SQL injection** (values are bound as data) and it's **faster for repeated execution** (parsed/planned once).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know PreparedStatement's two big wins: safety and reuse.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating it as security-only, or still concatenating values.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention it also handles type conversion and escaping correctly for you.

sections.title: What PreparedStatement Is and Why It's Preferred
sections.content:
A **`PreparedStatement`** is a **parameterized**, **precompiled** SQL statement. You write SQL with `?` placeholders and bind values with setters (`setInt`, `setString`). It beats a plain `Statement` on two fronts:

- **Security** — parameters are sent **separately** from the SQL, so input is treated as data, not code: **no SQL injection**.
- **Performance** — the DB parses and plans it **once**; repeated executions just rebind values.

It also handles **type conversion and escaping** for you (quotes, dates, NULLs), so you don't hand-format values into strings.

sections.title: PreparedStatement at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Safety|~injection-proof|? placeholders|values bound as data|SQL parsed first
blue|Performance|~precompiled|parse + plan once|rebind + run|fast in loops/batches
amber|Convenience|~handles formatting|type conversion|escaping quotes/dates|NULL handling
rose|vs Statement|~the default|Statement = static only|PreparedStatement = with input|always prefer

sections.title: PreparedStatement vs Statement
sections.content:
| Aspect | Statement | PreparedStatement |
|---|---|---|
| Parameters | none (concatenate) | `?` placeholders |
| SQL injection | vulnerable | safe |
| Precompiled | no | yes |
| Repeated execution | re-parsed each time | plan reused |
| Escaping/types | manual | automatic |

sections.title: Statement: concatenated, unsafe, re-parsed
sections.content:
```java
Statement st = con.createStatement();
String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"; // injectable
ResultSet rs = st.executeQuery(sql);  // re-parsed every call
```

sections.title: PreparedStatement: parameterized, safe, reusable
When to Use It
sections.content: Use **`PreparedStatement`** for essentially every query that has parameters or runs more than once — which is almost all real queries. Reserve plain `Statement` for static, parameterless one-off SQL like DDL.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **PreparedStatement** = parameterized (`?`) + precompiled SQL.
- **Prevents SQL injection** — values bound as data.
- **Faster for repeated execution** — parsed/planned once.
- **Handles escaping and type conversion** automatically.
- **The default** over `Statement` for any query with input.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: A PreparedStatement is a parameterized, precompiled SQL statement. You write the SQL with question-mark placeholders, and then bind the actual values using setter methods like setInt and setString. It's preferred over a plain Statement for two main reasons. The first is security: because the parameter values are sent to the database separately from the SQL text, the input is always treated as data rather than executable code, which completely prevents SQL injection. The second is performance: the database parses and builds the execution plan for a PreparedStatement once, and then every subsequent execution just rebinds the new values and reuses that plan, which makes it noticeably faster in loops and batches. There's a third, quieter benefit too: PreparedStatement handles type conversion and escaping for you. You don't have to worry about quoting strings, formatting dates, or escaping special characters, because the driver does it correctly based on the parameter type, including handling NULLs. So in practice I use PreparedStatement for essentially every query that has parameters or runs more than once, which is almost everything, and I only fall back to a plain Statement for static, parameterless one-off SQL like a CREATE TABLE.

beats.text: PreparedStatement is a precompiled SQL template. You write the SQL with ? as placeholders for values, then supply each value with a typed setter method. The database compiles the template once and reuses the plan on every execution.
It exists to solve two problems at once: security (SQL injection) and performance (plan caching). Statement with string concatenation has both problems; PreparedStatement has neither.

items: ? placeholder — marks every parameter position; 1-indexed
Typed setters — setString, setInt, setLong, setDate, setTimestamp, setNull; match the column's SQL type

questions.question: How do you use PreparedStatement for an INSERT query in JDBC?
questions.title: PreparedStatement for INSERT in JDBC
questions.direct_answer: To INSERT with a `PreparedStatement`: prepare the SQL with `?` placeholders, bind each value with the right setter (`setInt`, `setString`, `setBigDecimal`), then call **`executeUpdate()`**, which returns the number of rows inserted. Use try-with-resources to close it.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can write a parameterized INSERT correctly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Off-by-one on 1-based parameter indexes, or using executeQuery for an INSERT.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note parameter indices are 1-based and executeUpdate returns the affected-row count.

sections.title: Inserting with a PreparedStatement
sections.content:
An INSERT through a `PreparedStatement` follows a tidy recipe: write the SQL with `?` for each value, bind the values in order with the matching setters, and call **`executeUpdate()`** (not `executeQuery` — INSERT changes data). `executeUpdate` returns an **int**: the number of rows inserted.

Two details freshers trip on: parameter indices are **1-based** (the first `?` is index 1), and the setter must match the column type (`setInt`, `setString`, `setBigDecimal`, `setTimestamp`).

sections.title: Parameterized INSERT at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|SQL|~placeholders|INSERT ... VALUES (?, ?)|one ? per value|order matters
emerald|Bind|~typed setters|setInt/setString|1-based index|match column type
amber|Execute|~executeUpdate|returns int row count|not executeQuery|for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE
rose|Close|~try-with-resources|auto-close|no leaks|

sections.title: INSERT Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Code |
|---|---|
| 1 | `prepareStatement("INSERT INTO users (name, age) VALUES (?, ?)")` |
| 2 | `ps.setString(1, name)` |
| 3 | `ps.setInt(2, age)` |
| 4 | `int rows = ps.executeUpdate()` |

sections.title: A parameterized INSERT
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **0-based indexing**: the first `?` is index **1**, not 0.
- **`executeQuery` for INSERT**: use `executeUpdate` (returns row count).
- **Wrong setter for the type**: `setString` for a number column can fail or mis-store.
- **Not closing**: wrap in try-with-resources.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Prepare** SQL with one `?` per value.
- **Bind** with typed setters; indices are **1-based**.
- **`executeUpdate()`** runs the INSERT, returns rows affected.
- **Match the setter** to the column type.
- **try-with-resources** closes the statement.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Inserting a row with a PreparedStatement is a clean little recipe. First you prepare the SQL with question-mark placeholders, one for each value, for example INSERT INTO users, name, email, age, VALUES, question mark, question mark, question mark. Then you bind each value with the setter that matches its type: setString for the name and email, setInt for the age. The detail that trips up a lot of freshers is that the parameter indices are one-based, so the first question mark is index one, not zero. After binding all the parameters, you call executeUpdate, not executeQuery, because an INSERT changes data rather than returning rows. executeUpdate returns an int, which is the number of rows inserted, so for a single insert you'd expect it to return one. I always wrap the PreparedStatement in try-with-resources so it closes automatically. The main mistakes to watch for are using zero-based indexing out of habit, calling executeQuery on an insert, which is the wrong method, and using the wrong setter for the column type, like setString on a numeric column, which can fail or store the value incorrectly. So the summary is: prepare with placeholders, bind with one-based typed setters, and call executeUpdate.

beats.text: A PreparedStatement INSERT follows the same pattern as a SELECT but uses executeUpdate() instead of executeQuery(), and optionally requests the auto-generated primary key back from the database.
executeUpdate() signals to the driver that no ResultSet rows are expected back — just a count. The RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS flag tells the database to also return whatever auto-increment ID it assigned.

items: prepareStatement(sql, RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS) — asks the database to capture the generated ID
setXxx() calls — bind each column value by 1-based position
executeUpdate() — runs the INSERT; returns the number of rows inserted (usually 1)
getGeneratedKeys() — returns a ResultSet with the auto-increment ID; call next() then getLong(1)

beats.text: Inserting a new order: prepareStatement('INSERT INTO orders (customer_id, total) VALUES (?, ?)', RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS), setLong(1, customerId), setBigDecimal(2, total), executeUpdate() returns 1. Then getGeneratedKeys() gives a ResultSet; getLong(1) is the new order_id, which you immediately use to insert order line items. Using SELECT MAX(id) to get the generated key — another concurrent INSERT can get a higher ID first, giving you the wrong one.

questions.question: How do you set different data types in PreparedStatement?
questions.title: PreparedStatement Setter Methods for Different Data Types
questions.direct_answer: Bind each parameter with the **type-specific setter**: `setInt`, `setLong`, `setString`, `setBoolean`, `setBigDecimal` (for money), `setDate`/`setTimestamp` (for dates/times), and `setNull(index, Types.X)` for NULL. Match the setter to the column type so the driver converts and escapes correctly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the typed setters and how to bind NULL and dates correctly.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using setString for numbers/dates, or passing Java null instead of setNull.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use setBigDecimal for money and setTimestamp for datetimes; setNull for NULLs.

sections.title: Setting Different Data Types
sections.content:
`PreparedStatement` has a **typed setter for each SQL type**, and using the right one lets the driver convert and escape the value correctly:

- Numbers — `setInt`, `setLong`, `setDouble`, **`setBigDecimal`** (money/precision).
- Text — `setString`.
- Boolean — `setBoolean`.
- Dates/times — `setDate` (date only), **`setTimestamp`** (date + time).
- NULL — **`setNull(index, java.sql.Types.X)`** (don't rely on Java `null`).

Matching the setter to the column type avoids subtle bugs (string-stored numbers, lost time components, mis-handled NULLs).

sections.title: Typed Setters at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Numbers|~by precision|setInt/setLong|setDouble|setBigDecimal for money
emerald|Text/Bool|~basics|setString|setBoolean|
amber|Date/Time|~watch granularity|setDate = date only|setTimestamp = date+time|use java.sql types
rose|NULL|~explicit|setNull(idx, Types.X)|not bare null|specify the SQL type

sections.title: Setter Cheat Sheet
sections.content:
| Java/SQL type | Setter |
|---|---|
| int / Integer | `setInt` |
| money / decimal | `setBigDecimal` |
| String | `setString` |
| boolean | `setBoolean` |
| date+time | `setTimestamp` |
| NULL | `setNull(idx, Types.X)` |

sections.title: Binding several types (and NULL)
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`setString` for numbers/dates**: causes type mismatches or string-stored values.
- **`double` for money**: use `setBigDecimal` to avoid rounding errors.
- **Bare Java `null`**: prefer `setNull(idx, Types.X)` so the driver knows the type.
- **`setDate` when you need time**: use `setTimestamp` to keep the time component.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **One typed setter per SQL type** — match it to the column.
- **`setBigDecimal`** for money (avoid `double`).
- **`setTimestamp`** for date+time; `setDate` for date only.
- **`setNull(idx, Types.X)`** for NULL values.
- **Right setter** → correct conversion and escaping.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: PreparedStatement gives you a typed setter for each SQL data type, and using the correct one is important because it lets the driver convert and escape the value properly. For numbers you've got setInt, setLong, and setDouble, and for money or anything needing exact precision you should use setBigDecimal rather than a double, because doubles introduce rounding errors. For text it's setString, and for booleans setBoolean. Dates and times are a place people get tripped up: setDate stores just a date with no time component, while setTimestamp stores a full date and time, so if you need the time you use setTimestamp. And for NULL values, the right way is setNull, passing the parameter index and the SQL type from java dot sql dot Types, rather than relying on a bare Java null, because the driver needs to know what type the NULL is. Matching the setter to the column type avoids a bunch of subtle bugs, like a number getting stored as a string, the time portion of a datetime getting silently dropped, or NULLs being mishandled. So my rule is simple: pick the setter that matches the column's type, use setBigDecimal for money, setTimestamp for datetimes, and setNull for nulls, and the driver takes care of the conversion and escaping for you.

questions.question: How does PreparedStatement prevent SQL injection?
questions.title: How PreparedStatement Prevents SQL Injection
questions.direct_answer: **PreparedStatement** prevents SQL injection because the SQL is **parsed and compiled with placeholders first**, and parameter values are then **bound as data**, never as part of the query text. So even malicious input like `' OR '1'='1` is treated as a literal value and can't change the query's structure.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can explain the parse-then-bind mechanism, not just say 'it's safe'.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking PreparedStatement 'escapes' input rather than separating code from data.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Clarify the query structure is fixed at prepare time, before any value is bound.

sections.title: How PreparedStatement Stops Injection
sections.content:
The protection comes from **separating code from data**. When you prepare a `PreparedStatement`, the database **parses and compiles the SQL with `?` placeholders** — the **query structure is fixed at this point**, before any value exists. Then `setString`/`setInt` **bind the values as data** into those slots.

Because the structure is already locked in, a value like `' OR '1'='1` is just a string compared against a column — it can't add clauses or change logic. It's not about escaping characters; it's that **input never reaches the SQL parser**.

sections.title: Why It's Safe
sections.content:
blue|Prepare|~structure fixed|parse + compile with ?|before values exist|query shape locked
emerald|Bind|~data only|setString/setInt|values into slots|never parsed as SQL
rose|Attack input|~harmless|' OR '1'='1|treated as a literal|can't add clauses
amber|Key idea|~code vs data|not escaping|separation|input never hits parser

sections.title: Concatenation: input IS the query
PreparedStatement: structure fixed before the value
Where This Applies
sections.content: Use parameter binding for **all** user-controlled input that reaches SQL. PreparedStatement handles **values** safely, but it does **not** parameterize identifiers like table/column names or `ORDER BY` directions — those must be validated against a whitelist, since they can't be bound as `?`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Parse first, bind second** — structure fixed before values exist.
- **Values are data**, never part of the SQL text.
- **`' OR '1'='1`** becomes a harmless literal.
- **It's separation of code/data**, not character escaping.
- **Identifiers** (table/column names) can't be bound — whitelist them.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: PreparedStatement prevents SQL injection through separation of code and data, and it helps to explain the mechanism rather than just saying it's safe. When you prepare a PreparedStatement, the database parses and compiles the SQL with the question-mark placeholders in place. The crucial point is that the structure of the query is fixed at that moment, before any actual value exists. Then, when you call setString or setInt, the values are bound into those placeholder slots as pure data. Because the query's structure is already locked in, a malicious value like quote OR one equals one is just treated as a literal string to compare against a column; it can't add a new clause, close a quote, or change the logic, so it simply matches nobody. A subtle but important clarification: this isn't really about escaping special characters. It's that the input never reaches the SQL parser at all; it only ever flows in as a bound value. One caveat worth raising to show depth: PreparedStatement only parameterizes values, not identifiers. So you can't bind a table name, a column name, or an ORDER BY direction with a question mark. If any of those need to be dynamic based on user input, you have to validate them against a whitelist of allowed values, because they can't be protected by parameter binding.

speakable_v2.hook: PreparedStatement doesn't escape your input — it locks the query's shape before the value arrives, so ' OR '1'='1 has nowhere to go.

beats.text: PreparedStatement uses a two-phase database protocol. Phase one: the SQL template is sent to the database, parsed, and compiled into a fixed execution plan. Phase two: parameter values are sent separately and bound into the pre-compiled slots as literal data.
SQL injection is possible only when user input can change the SQL structure. By fixing the structure in phase one before any user data arrives, PreparedStatement closes that gap completely.

items: Phase 1 — SQL template sent to DB, parsed, compiled; structure is now fixed
Phase 2 — parameter values sent, bound as literal data into the fixed slots
Result — even if a value contains 'OR 1=1' it's just a string; the query structure can't change
Manual escaping comparison — unreliable; edge cases in escape logic are how injections get through

beats.text: Fetching orders by customer name: prepareStatement('SELECT id FROM orders WHERE customer_name = ?'), setString(1, userInput). If userInput is 'Smith' OR 1=1 --, the database receives it as a literal string value bound to position 1. The WHERE clause looks for a customer named exactly 'Smith' OR 1=1 --' — which matches nothing. Under Statement with concatenation, the same input would terminate the quote, add the OR clause, and return every order. [depth: how the database's wire protocol encodes parameter values separately from the SQL statement in server-side prepared statements]

items: Concatenating user input into the SQL template itself before calling prepareStatement — PreparedStatement can't protect code that was already vulnerable before it was called.
Thinking manual escaping is equivalent — regex-based escaping has been bypassed in real-world attacks; two-phase binding hasn't.

speakable_v2.cap: Two-phase binding is why PreparedStatement is injection-proof. The structure is locked before any data arrives.

questions.question: How do you execute a batch of INSERT statements using PreparedStatement?
questions.title: Batch Inserts with PreparedStatement
questions.direct_answer: To batch INSERTs: prepare the INSERT once, loop setting parameters and calling **`addBatch()`** for each row, then call **`executeBatch()`** to send them together. Wrap it in a transaction (auto-commit off, commit at end) and flush large batches periodically to control memory.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can write a correct batched-insert loop.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling executeUpdate inside the loop instead of addBatch, or never committing.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Flush every N rows and commit once; handle rollback on failure.

sections.title: Executing a Batch of INSERTs
sections.content:
Batching many inserts is a standard pattern: **prepare the INSERT once**, then for each row bind the parameters and call **`addBatch()`** (queue, don't execute). After the loop — or every N rows — call **`executeBatch()`** to send the queued rows in one round-trip.

Do it inside a **transaction**: `setAutoCommit(false)`, run the batch, then `commit()` once. On error, `rollback()`. Flush periodically (e.g. every 1,000 rows) so a giant batch doesn't blow up memory.

sections.title: Batch INSERT at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Prepare once|~outside loop|one PreparedStatement|reuse for all rows|
emerald|addBatch|~per row|bind then addBatch|queues the row|no round-trip
amber|executeBatch|~send together|one round-trip|flush every N|returns int[]
rose|Transaction|~atomic + fast|auto-commit off|commit once|rollback on error

sections.title: Batch INSERT Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Code |
|---|---|
| 1 | `con.setAutoCommit(false)` |
| 2 | `prepareStatement("INSERT ... VALUES (?, ?)")` once |
| 3 | loop: `setXxx(...)`, `addBatch()`, flush every N |
| 4 | `executeBatch()`, then `con.commit()` |

sections.title: Batched INSERT loop
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **`executeUpdate` in the loop**: defeats batching — use `addBatch`.
- **Re-preparing per row**: prepare once outside the loop.
- **No commit / auto-commit on**: each item commits separately.
- **One enormous batch**: flush every N rows to bound memory.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Prepare once**, `addBatch()` per row, `executeBatch()` to send.
- **Wrap in a transaction**: auto-commit off, commit once.
- **Flush every N rows** to control memory.
- **`rollback()`** on failure.
- **Far fewer round-trips** than per-row inserts.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: To execute a batch of inserts efficiently, the pattern is to prepare the insert statement once, then loop over your data, and for each row bind the parameters and call addBatch instead of executing. addBatch just queues that row; it doesn't go to the database yet. After the loop, you call executeBatch, which sends all the queued rows together in essentially one round-trip, and that's what makes it fast compared to inserting row by row. I always run this inside a transaction: I set auto-commit to false before the loop, run the batch, and commit once at the end, which is both faster and atomic. If anything throws, I roll back. For large datasets I also flush periodically, calling executeBatch every thousand rows or so, so the batch doesn't grow huge and exhaust memory, and then I flush any remaining rows after the loop. The mistakes to avoid are calling executeUpdate inside the loop, which defeats the whole purpose of batching; re-preparing the statement on every iteration instead of once outside the loop; and leaving auto-commit on, because then each batch item commits separately and you lose most of the benefit. So the recipe is: prepare once, addBatch per row, flush every N rows, executeBatch the rest, and commit once.

seo.metaTitle: Batch INSERT with PreparedStatement | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: How to do batch inserts with PreparedStatement: addBatch(), executeBatch(), auto-commit handling. Java backend fresher interview answer on JDBC batch operations.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app connecting to a MySQL database with JDBC to query an orders table
speakable_v2.hook: A correct batch insert prepares once, queues with addBatch, fires with executeBatch, and commits a single time — not once per row.

beats.text: Batch inserts queue multiple parameter sets with addBatch() and flush them in one network call with executeBatch(). Wrapping everything in a manual transaction makes it atomic and fast.
Each individual executeUpdate() call is a full database round trip. For thousands of rows, that latency accumulates. Batching groups many rows into one call and one commit.

items: setAutoCommit(false) — disables per-statement commits; you control the transaction boundary
addBatch() — queues current parameter set; doesn't execute
executeBatch() every 500-1000 rows — flushes to DB and frees memory
clearBatch() — resets the queue after each flush
conn.commit() at the end — all rows in one atomic transaction
conn.rollback() on exception — nothing is committed if something fails

beats.text: Importing 50,000 orders from a CSV: disable auto-commit, loop through rows calling setLong/setBigDecimal/addBatch, flush every 1,000 rows with executeBatch + clearBatch, commit at the end, rollback in the catch block. Network round trips drop from 50,000 to about 50. In Spring Boot, JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate() handles the auto-commit toggle and clearBatch for you. [depth: how MySQL's rewriteBatchedStatements=true rewrites batched INSERTs into a single multi-row INSERT for further performance]

items: Not disabling auto-commit — each addBatch silently commits immediately, negating the batch transaction and adding per-row commit overhead.
Not calling clearBatch after executeBatch — the queue grows unbounded and risks OutOfMemoryError on large datasets.

speakable_v2.cap: Batch pattern: disable auto-commit, addBatch in a loop, flush every 1000 rows, commit at the end. Spring's batchUpdate wraps this cleanly.

questions.question: How do you retrieve auto-generated keys after an INSERT with PreparedStatement?
questions.title: Retrieving Auto-Generated Keys
questions.direct_answer: Request generated keys at prepare time with `prepareStatement(sql, Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS)`, run `executeUpdate()`, then call **`getGeneratedKeys()`** to get a `ResultSet` containing the auto-increment key(s). Read the key with `rs.next()` and `rs.getLong(1)`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know the RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS + getGeneratedKeys flow.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Re-querying with a SELECT to find the new id instead of using getGeneratedKeys.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note you must opt in at prepare time and the key comes back as a ResultSet.

sections.title: Retrieving Auto-Generated Keys
sections.content:
When you INSERT into a table with an **auto-increment** primary key, you often need the **new id** immediately (to return it or link related rows). JDBC gives it to you without a second query:

1. **Opt in at prepare time**: `con.prepareStatement(sql, Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS)`.
2. **`executeUpdate()`** the INSERT.
3. **`getGeneratedKeys()`** — returns a `ResultSet` of the generated key(s).
4. **Read it**: `rs.next(); long id = rs.getLong(1);`.

Don't run a separate `SELECT MAX(id)` — that's racy and wrong under concurrency.

sections.title: Generated Keys at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Opt in|~at prepare time|RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS|second arg|required
emerald|Execute|~normal INSERT|executeUpdate()|inserts the row|
amber|getGeneratedKeys|~returns ResultSet|the new key(s)|rs.getLong(1)|1-based column
rose|Don't|~no SELECT MAX|racy under concurrency|use generated keys|reliable

sections.title: Generated Keys Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Code |
|---|---|
| 1 | `prepareStatement(sql, Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS)` |
| 2 | `ps.setXxx(...)`, `ps.executeUpdate()` |
| 3 | `ResultSet keys = ps.getGeneratedKeys()` |
| 4 | `if (keys.next()) long id = keys.getLong(1)` |

sections.title: Getting the new auto-increment id
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting `RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS`**: `getGeneratedKeys()` returns nothing without it.
- **`SELECT MAX(id)` after insert**: racy under concurrency — may return another session's id.
- **Not calling `keys.next()`**: the keys come back as a ResultSet you must advance.
- **Assuming column name**: read by index `getLong(1)` (key column naming varies).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Opt in** with `Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS` at prepare time.
- **`getGeneratedKeys()`** returns a `ResultSet` of the new key(s).
- **Read** with `keys.next()` then `getLong(1)`.
- **Never** use `SELECT MAX(id)` — it's racy.
- **Read by index**, since the key column name varies.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: When you insert a row into a table with an auto-increment primary key, you usually need the newly generated id right away, for example to return it to the caller or to insert related child rows. JDBC lets you get it without running a second query. The first step is to opt in when you prepare the statement, by passing Statement dot RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS as the second argument to prepareStatement. This tells the driver to capture the generated keys. Then you set your parameters and call executeUpdate as normal to perform the insert. After that, you call getGeneratedKeys on the statement, which returns a ResultSet containing the generated key or keys. You advance it with next and read the value, typically with getLong of column index one. The important anti-pattern to avoid is running a separate SELECT MAX of id after the insert to figure out the new id; that's racy under concurrency, because another session could have inserted in between, and you'd get the wrong id. Using getGeneratedKeys is reliable because it returns the key generated by your specific insert. Two small details: you must remember to pass RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS at prepare time or getGeneratedKeys comes back empty, and you should read the key by column index rather than by name, since the name of the key column varies across databases.

questions.question: What is CallableStatement and when do you use it?
questions.title: CallableStatement for Stored Procedures
questions.direct_answer: A **CallableStatement** (a subtype of `PreparedStatement`) is used to call **stored procedures** via the `{call proc(?, ?)}` escape syntax. It supports **IN**, **OUT**, and **INOUT** parameters — register OUT params with `registerOutParameter` before executing, then read them afterward.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know CallableStatement is for stored procedures with IN/OUT params.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to register OUT parameters, or using it for plain queries.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention it extends PreparedStatement and when stored procedures are appropriate.

sections.title: What CallableStatement Is
sections.content:
**`CallableStatement`** extends `PreparedStatement` and is JDBC's way to invoke **stored procedures** (and functions). You create it with `con.prepareCall("{call proc(?, ?)}")` using the JDBC escape syntax.

Procedures support three parameter directions: **IN** (you set), **OUT** (the procedure returns), **INOUT** (both). For each OUT param you must **`registerOutParameter(idx, Types.X)`** *before* `execute()`, then read it with the matching getter afterward. Use stored procedures when logic genuinely belongs in the database; keep ordinary CRUD in the app.

sections.title: CallableStatement at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|What|~calls procedures|prepareCall|{call proc(?,?)}|extends PreparedStatement
emerald|Params|~three directions|IN you set|OUT you read|INOUT both
amber|OUT|~register first|registerOutParameter|before execute|read after
rose|When|~DB-side logic|shared across apps|heavy data ops|not for plain CRUD

sections.title: CallableStatement Recipe
sections.content:
| Step | Code |
|---|---|
| 1 | `con.prepareCall("{call proc(?, ?)}")` |
| 2 | set IN params |
| 3 | `registerOutParameter(idx, Types.X)` |
| 4 | `execute()` |
| 5 | read OUT params |

sections.title: Calling a procedure with IN and OUT params
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Skipping `registerOutParameter`**: OUT values can't be read.
- **Using it for plain queries**: that's `PreparedStatement`'s job.
- **Wrong index/type**: indices are 1-based; OUT type must match.
- **Overusing procedures**: business logic in the DB is harder to test/version.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **CallableStatement** calls stored procedures; extends `PreparedStatement`.
- **Escape syntax**: `{call proc(?, ?)}` via `prepareCall`.
- **IN / OUT / INOUT** parameter directions.
- **Register OUT params** before execute; read after.
- **Use for** DB-side logic, not ordinary CRUD.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: CallableStatement is a subtype of PreparedStatement that you use specifically to call stored procedures and functions in the database. You create one with connection dot prepareCall, using the JDBC escape syntax, which is curly brace call, the procedure name, and question marks for parameters. What makes it different from a regular PreparedStatement is support for parameter directions. A stored procedure can have IN parameters that you set as inputs, OUT parameters that the procedure returns to you, and INOUT parameters that do both. For each OUT parameter, you have to call registerOutParameter, passing the parameter index and its SQL type, before you execute, and then after executing you read the value with the matching getter like getLong. So the recipe is prepareCall, set your IN parameters, register your OUT parameters, call execute, and read the OUT values. The common mistakes are forgetting to register the OUT parameters, which means you can't read them, and using CallableStatement for ordinary queries, which is really PreparedStatement's job. On the design side, stored procedures make sense when the logic genuinely belongs in the database, like operations shared across multiple applications or heavy data processing, but I avoid pushing too much business logic into procedures, because it's harder to test and version-control than application code.

beats.text: CallableStatement extends PreparedStatement specifically to call stored procedures and functions. Its main addition is OUT parameter support — after execute(), the database writes result values back into the statement for you to read.

Stored procedures often return multiple values or perform multi-step database work in a single call. PreparedStatement can only receive rows via ResultSet; CallableStatement adds the ability to receive scalar output values directly.

items: prepareCall('{call proc(?, ?)}') — JDBC escape syntax; works across MySQL, PostgreSQL, and Oracle
setXxx() for IN parameters — same as PreparedStatement
registerOutParameter(position, Types.XXX) — declared before execute(); required for each OUT parameter
execute() — runs the procedure
getXxx(position) — reads OUT values after execute()

beats.text: A MySQL procedure count_orders_for_department takes a department name (IN) and returns a count (OUT). Java: prepareCall('{call count_orders_for_department(?, ?)}'), setString(1, 'Engineering'), registerOutParameter(2, Types.INTEGER), execute(), getInt(2) returns the count. Spring's SimpleJdbcCall removes the escape syntax and parameter registration boilerplate. [depth: how CallableStatement.registerOutParameter informs the JDBC driver to allocate a slot for the database's response value]

items: Forgetting registerOutParameter before execute() — the driver doesn't know an output is expected and you get a null or exception.
Using PreparedStatement for a procedure with OUT parameters — it silently discards the output; you'll get no data back.
